(Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from genetic data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The OAS family in humans is comprised of three catalytically active OAS proteins: OAS1, OAS2, and OAS3.
claims.source: In humans, the OAS family is comprised of three catalytically active OAS proteins: OAS1, OAS2, and OAS3.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of the OAS family.

claims.claim: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain.
claims.source: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain, while OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of this unit, and OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of this unit (Hornung et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of the OAS1 unit.
claims.source: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain, while OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of this unit, and OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of this unit (Hornung et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of the OAS1 unit.
claims.source: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain, while OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of this unit, and OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of this unit (Hornung et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: OAS proteins have different RNA binding capabilities and favor synthesis of different lengths of 2′−5′A.
claims.source: Although the OAS proteins have different RNA binding capabilities and favor synthesis of different lengths of 2′−5′A (Ibsen et al., 2014), we demonstrate a novel mechanism where subcellular localization determines the antiviral specificity of these proteins.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Subcellular localization determines the antiviral specificity of OAS proteins.
claims.source: Although the OAS proteins have different RNA binding capabilities and favor synthesis of different lengths of 2′−5′A (Ibsen et al., 2014), we demonstrate a novel mechanism where subcellular localization determines the antiviral specificity of these proteins.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential antiviral activity based on localization.

claims.claim: 2′−5′A locally activates RNase L around sites of viral replication.
claims.source: Based on the reduction of vRNA in our study, we propose a model in which 2′−5′A locally activates RNase L around sites of viral replication.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation from experimental observations.

claims.claim: The A allele at rs10774671 is associated with multiple autoimmune disorders.
claims.source: This is further supported by the genetic association of the A allele with multiple autoimmune disorders, as enhanced immune responses are sometimes made at a tradeoff for overall host fitness (Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claims.claim: By positioning viral RNA sensors at different subcellular sites, the host can potentially respond to diverse replication strategies.
claims.source: By positioning viral RNA sensors at different subcellular sites of viral RNA accumulation, the host can potentially respond to diverse replication strategies in the cytosol, nucleus, or on intracellular membranes.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and knowledge of viral replication.

claims.claim: Subcellular targeting is likely important for function of other OAS proteins.
claims.source: Although this work focused on OAS1 and the detection of viral nucleic acids, subcellular targeting is likely also important for function of other OAS proteins.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation from findings about OAS1.

claims.claim: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini.
claims.source: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini, suggesting the CaaX motif has a conserved role in the function of OAS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: The CaaX motif has a conserved role in the function of OAS1 across vertebrate species.
claims.source: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini, suggesting the CaaX motif has a conserved role in the function of OAS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Inferred from conservation of CaaX motif across species.

claims.claim: The A549 cell line carries only the A allele at rs10774671.
claims.source: Genotyping revealed that the A549 cell line carried only the A allele, that PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carried both the A and G alleles, and that Daudi cells carried only the G allele at rs10774671 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by genotyping data.

claims.claim: PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carry both the A and G alleles at rs10774671.
claims.source: Genotyping revealed that the A549 cell line carried only the A allele, that PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carried both the A and G alleles, and that Daudi cells carried only the G allele at rs10774671 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by genotyping data.

claims.claim: Daudi cells carry only the G allele at rs10774671.
claims.source: Genotyping revealed that the A549 cell line carried only the A allele, that PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carried both the A and G alleles, and that Daudi cells carried only the G allele at rs10774671 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by genotyping data.

claims.claim: Two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa were detected in cells with at least one copy of the G allele.
claims.source: We detected two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa in cells with at least one copy of the G allele, while only p42 or p46 were expressed in A/A or G/G cells, respectively (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Only p42 is expressed in A/A cells at rs10774671.
claims.source: We detected two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa in cells with at least one copy of the G allele, while only p42 or p46 were expressed in A/A or G/G cells, respectively (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Only p46 is expressed in G/G cells at rs10774671.
claims.source: We detected two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa in cells with at least one copy of the G allele, while only p42 or p46 were expressed in A/A or G/G cells, respectively (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: The p44, p48, and p52 isoforms were not observed under the experimental conditions used.
claims.source: We did not observe the expression of other OAS1 isoforms under these conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing only p42 and p46.

claims.claim: Cells homozygous for the A allele at rs10774671 only produce p42.
claims.source: Cells homozygous for the A allele only produced p42, while cells homozygous for the G allele only produced p46 (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from PBMCs.

claims.claim: Cells homozygous for the G allele at rs10774671 only produce p46.
claims.source: Cells homozygous for the A allele only produced p42, while cells homozygous for the G allele only produced p46 (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from PBMCs.

claims.claim: PBMCs harboring at least one G allele express p46 stronger than p42.
claims.source: Corroborating our findings, PBMCs harboring at least one G allele expressed p46 stronger than p42, which may be influenced by splice site preference or mRNA stability.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from PBMCs.

claims.claim: The p44, p48, and p52 isoforms are weakly expressed at the mRNA level and unstable at the protein level.
claims.source: We did not observe expression of the p44, p48, or p52 isoforms in any of the cells used in this study, which is consistent with previous reports demonstrating that these isoforms are weakly expressed at the mRNA level, and unstable at the protein level (Carey et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: CaaX motifs with a leucine in the 'X' position are preferentially geranylgeranylated by GGTaseI.
claims.source: Depending on the identity of the 'X' amino acid, CaaX-containing proteins can be either farnesylated or geranylgeranylated by the respective farnesyl or geranylgeranyl transferases. CaaX motifs with a leucine in the 'X' position, as in the case of p46, are preferentially geranylgeranylated by geranylgeranyl transferase I (GGTaseI) (Hartman et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on prenylation.

claims.claim: EMCV is a positive-strand RNA virus in the picornavirus family that replicates on ER and Golgi membranes.
claims.source: Encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) is a positive-strand RNA virus in the picornavirus family, which replicates on organelles of the endomembrane system, particularly ER and Golgi membranes, and is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway (Chebath et al., 1987; Melia et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: EMCV is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway.
claims.source: Encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) is a positive-strand RNA virus in the picornavirus family, which replicates on organelles of the endomembrane system, particularly ER and Golgi membranes, and is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway (Chebath et al., 1987; Melia et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: The antiviral activity of p44, p48, and p52 against EMCV is inferior to p46.
claims.source: We also compared the antiviral activity of p44, p48, and p52 against EMCV over a range of doses and found their antiviral activity was inferior to p46 (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claims.claim: Among OAS1 isoforms, OAS1 p46 confers the strongest antiviral activity against EMCV.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that, among OAS1 isoforms, OAS1 p46 confers the strongest antiviral activity against EMCV.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparative antiviral activity data across all isoforms.

claims.claim: Complementing RNASEL KO cells with RNase L and p46 significantly reduces EMCV RNA and titer.
claims.source: RNASEL KO 293 T cells complemented with RNase L and expressing p46 showed a significant reduction in EMCV RNA and titer over control.
claims.evidence: Supported by complementation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E and F.

claims.claim: Cleavage of cellular RNA by RNase L generates immunostimulatory RNAs that are sensed by RIG-I and MDA5.
claims.source: Cleavage of cellular RNA by RNase L has been shown to generate immunostimulatory RNAs that are sensed by RIG-I and MDA5 and increase antiviral protection through the production of interferon (Malathi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: During picornavirus infection, ER- and Golgi-derived membranes form replication organelles that are sites of vRNA replication.
claims.source: During picornavirus infection, ER- and Golgi-derived membranes form replication organelles that are sites of vRNA replication (Melia et al., 2019; Melia et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: Endomembrane localization of p46 places this viral RNA sensor on membranes utilized by EMCV for replication.
claims.source: Therefore, we hypothesized that endomembrane localization of p46 places this viral RNA sensor on membranes utilized by EMCV for replication and would allow the enhanced access of p46 to EMCV RNA.
claims.evidence: Based on hypothesis from knowledge of EMCV replication and p46 localization.

claims.claim: OAS1 p46 is in close proximity to sites of EMCV RNA replication where dsRNA ligands are present.
claims.source: These data suggest that p46 is in close proximity to sites of EMCV RNA replication where dsRNA ligands are present.
claims.evidence: Inferred from microscopy data showing p46 colocalization with dsRNA.

claims.claim: OAS1 common+CTIL does not confer significantly increased antiviral activity over empty vector control.
claims.source: At similar protein expression levels, OAS1 common+CTIL did not confer significantly increased antiviral activity over the empty vector control and showed RNA levels similar to those in cells expressing the p42 isoform (Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claims.claim: OAS1 common+CTIL shows significantly decreased co-localization with Golgi membranes compared to p46.
claims.source: Interestingly, the OAS1 common+CTIL variant showed significantly decreased co-localization with Golgi membranes compared to p46 and appeared cytosolic and nuclear, as observed above for CaaX-deficient p42 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claims.claim: Other features in the unique C-termini of OAS1 p42 and p46 contribute to their individual antiviral activity.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest other features in the unique C-termini of OAS1 p42 and p46 contribute to their individual antiviral activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments showing CaaX motif alone is not sufficient.

claims.claim: None of the alanine substitution mutants in the p46 C-terminus affected viral RNA levels as strongly as disruption of the CaaX motif.
claims.source: Nevertheless, none of the alanine substitution mutants affected EMCV RNA levels as strongly as the disruption of the CaaX motif in p46ATIL.
claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for alanine mutants.

claims.claim: The E392-E/N393-D/N394 sequence is conserved in most mammalian OAS1 p46 orthologous isoforms.
claims.source: In fact, the E392-E/N393-D/N394 sequence is conserved in most mammalian OAS1 p46 orthologous isoforms, which suggests a possible function for this motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: OAS1 p46 mutant eight shows a slight but significant decrease in co-localization with Golgin-97 compared to p46.
claims.source: Although OAS1 p46 mutant eight localized to the Golgi, compared with p46, this mutant showed a slight but significant decrease in its co-localization with Golgin-97 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claims.claim: Tetramerization of OAS1 has been proposed as a requirement for synthesis of 2′−5′A.
claims.source: Tetramerization of OAS1 has been proposed as a requirement for synthesis of the second messenger 2′−5′A, indicating that several OAS1 molecules in close proximity are required to induce 2′−5′A synthesis upon viral RNA binding and to subsequently activate the RNase L pathway (Ghosh et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: CFK-mediated oligomerization is required for optimal EMCV RNA binding of OAS1 p46.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that CFK-mediated oligomerization is required for optimal EMCV RNA binding of OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: Mutation of the CFK motif does not alter the localization of p42 or p46.
claims.source: Importantly, mutation of the CFK motif did not alter the localization of either isoform (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claims.claim: The Δ22aa and Δ32aa deletion mutants have similar antiviral activities as p42CTIL.
claims.source: The Δ22aa and Δ32aa deletion mutants had similar antiviral activities as p42CTIL, which is identical in length to the Δ32aa mutant (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claims.claim: All p46 truncation mutants localize to the Golgi.
claims.source: Similar to p46, all the p46 truncation mutants localized to the Golgi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claims.claim: There is a slight but significant decrease in the correlation of p46 Δ32aa with the Golgi.
claims.source: However, there was a slight but significant decrease in the correlation of p46 Δ32aa with the Golgi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis from microscopy data.

claims.claim: The length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence is important for its antiviral activity.
claims.source: These data are consistent with our hypothesis that the length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence is important for increased antiviral activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments with chimeric proteins from different species.

claims.claim: Cow and fox OAS1 chimeras mimic human OAS1 p46 antiviral activity.
claims.source: We found cow and fox OAS1 chimeras mimicked human OAS1 p46 antiviral activity, whereas the shorter C-terminus of flying fox led to decreased antiviral activity of the chimeric protein compared to human OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for chimeric proteins.

claims.claim: The shorter C-terminus of flying fox OAS1 leads to decreased antiviral activity compared to human OAS1 p46.
claims.source: We found cow and fox OAS1 chimeras mimicked human OAS1 p46 antiviral activity, whereas the shorter C-terminus of flying fox led to decreased antiviral activity of the chimeric protein compared to human OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for chimeric proteins.

claims.claim: The alligator OAS1 p46 chimeric protein fails to exhibit similar antiviral activity as human OAS1 p46.

claims.evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for chimeric proteins.

claims.claim: The alligator and guinea pig lack conservation of the E392-E/N393-D/N394 motif proximal to the CaaX motif.
claims.source: Upon close examination, we found that the alligator (and guinea pig) lack conservation of the E392-E/N393-D/N394 motif proximal to the CaaX motif, which we have shown is required for strong antiviral activity (Figure 5A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: The length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence, CFK oligomerization domain, and potentially E-E/N-D/N sequence are required for enhanced antiviral activity of OAS1 p46.
claims.source: These data suggest that the length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence, CFK oligomerization domain, and potentially E-E/N-D/N sequence are required for enhanced antiviral activity of OAS1 p46.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments testing different C-terminal features.

claims.claim: West Nile virus replicates on membranes of the endomembrane system, primarily ER-derived membranes.
claims.source: WNV, like all flaviviruses, replicates on membranes of the endomembrane system, primarily ER-derived membranes (Westaway et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: OAS1 p46 is recruited to sites of WNV replication.

claims.claim: WNV infection causes a significant decrease in the association of p46 with Golgin-97.

claims.evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis from microscopy data.

claims.claim: OAS1 p46 may be recruited from the Golgi to sites of WNV replication.
claims.source: This suggests that p46 may be recruited from the Golgi to sites of WNV replication and is consistent with previous observations that Golgi membranes and proteins, including RNA binding proteins, are recruited to the replication organelles of flaviviruses (Ward et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from microscopy data and citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: OAS1 p46 localizes to ZIKV replication sites at the ER.
claims.source: We observed p46, but not p42, localized to ZIKV replication sites at the ER (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data during ZIKV infection.

claims.claim: Endomembrane localization of OAS1 p46 allows this protein to access sites of flavivirus RNA replication.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that endomembrane localization of OAS1 p46 allows this protein to access sites of flavivirus RNA replication.
claims.evidence: Inferred from microscopy data showing p46 localization to WNV and ZIKV replication sites.

claims.claim: CVB3 replicates within modified Golgi membranes.
claims.source: The human pathogenic picornavirus coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) replicates within modified Golgi membranes, and thus p46 may also be positioned to readily sense CVB3 RNA (Melia et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claims.claim: OAS1 p46 may have broad antiviral activity against members of the picornavirus family.
claims.source: These data suggest that OAS1 p46 may have broad antiviral activity against members of the picornavirus family, while p42 is less effective.
claims.evidence: Inferred from antiviral activity data against EMCV and CVB3.

claims.claim: Coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 use the endomembrane system for replication using primarily ER-derived membranes.
claims.source: Coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 use the endomembrane system for replication using primarily ER-derived membranes (Romero-Brey and Bartenschlager, 2014; Snijder et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claims.claim: IAV replicates within the nucleus.

results.result: OAS1 p46 is the only OAS1 isoform with a C-terminal CaaX motif (CTIL) and is geranylgeranylated at this motif. The CaaX motif is both necessary and sufficient for geranylgeranylation of OAS1.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C18, C19 are directly supported by click chemistry assay data (Figure 1D) showing geranylgeranylation of p46 and p42CTIL but not p42 or p46ATIL. The CaaX motif structure (C12, C13) and its preferential geranylgeranylation (C112) are supported by sequence data and established literature on prenylation.

results.result: OAS1 p46 localizes to the trans-Golgi network via its CaaX motif, while p42 localizes to the cytosol and nucleus. The CaaX motif is both necessary and sufficient for Golgi localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization with Golgin-97 (Figures 1E-H). Experiments with p46ATIL (CaaX mutant) and p42CTIL (CaaX addition) demonstrate necessity and sufficiency of the CaaX motif for Golgi localization.

results.result: OAS1 p46 has significantly enhanced antiviral activity against EMCV compared to p42 and other OAS1 isoforms. p46 reduces EMCV RNA by 50-fold and titer by 100-fold compared to control, and 10-fold and 50-fold respectively compared to p42.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27, C115-C116 are supported by RT-qPCR and plaque assay data (Figure 2B-C), siRNA knockdown experiments in THP-1 cells (Figure 2G), and experiments in primary human fibroblasts with different genotypes (Figure 2H-I). The data consistently show superior antiviral activity of p46 across multiple experimental systems.

results.result: The antiviral activity of both OAS1 p42 and p46 against EMCV requires catalytic activity for 2′-5′A synthesis and RNase L. Both isoforms have similar catalytic capacity, and the CaaX motif does not alter catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are supported by experiments with catalytic mutants (Figure 3B-C), RNase L knockout and complementation experiments (Figure 3E-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F), and in vitro 2′-5′A synthesis assays (Figure 3G). The data demonstrate that both isoforms require the same enzymatic pathway despite their differential antiviral potency.

results.result: OAS1 p42 and p46 confer antiviral activity against EMCV independent of IRF3-induced factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by experiments in IRF3 knockout cells (Figure 3I) showing that p46 retains significant antiviral activity in the absence of IRF3. This demonstrates that the differential antiviral activity is not due to secondary interferon responses.

results.result: During EMCV infection, OAS1 p46 redistributes to sites of viral dsRNA replication and has enhanced access to viral RNA compared to p42. The CaaX motif is required for p46 to bind EMCV RNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40, C121 are supported by confocal microscopy showing p46 colocalization with dsRNA during EMCV infection (Figure 4A) and RNA immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4B) demonstrating that p46 binds more EMCV RNA than p42, and that mutation of the CaaX motif (p46ATIL) abolishes this enhanced binding.

results.result: The CaaX motif is necessary but not sufficient for optimal antiviral activity of OAS1 against EMCV. Mutation of the CaaX motif in p46 reduces its antiviral activity to p42 levels, but addition of the CaaX motif to p42 does not enhance its activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44, C122-C124 are supported by viral RNA and titer data (Figure 4D-E, 4G-H) showing that p46ATIL has reduced activity while p42CTIL and OAS1 common+CTIL do not gain enhanced activity. This indicates that additional features in the p46 C-terminus beyond the CaaX motif contribute to its superior antiviral function.

results.result: The CFK oligomerization motif (C331F332K333) is critical for OAS1 antiviral activity. Disruption of this motif completely abolishes p42 antiviral activity but p46 retains residual activity similar to wild-type p42. CFK-mediated oligomerization is required for optimal EMCV RNA binding by p46.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50, C129 are supported by viral RNA quantification data for CFK mutants (Figure 5D-E), RNA immunoprecipitation data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), and established literature on OAS1 oligomerization. The differential dependence on the CFK motif between p42 and p46 suggests that membrane localization provides an alternative mechanism for p46 function.

results.result: The C-terminal length of p46 is important for its antiviral activity. C-terminal truncation mutants show length-dependent decreases in antiviral activity. Cross-species chimera experiments support the importance of C-terminal length and the conserved E-E/N-D/N motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52, C134-C139 are supported by viral RNA quantification data for truncation mutants (Figure 5G-H) and species chimeras (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J). The data show that shorter C-termini correlate with reduced antiviral activity, and that the E392-E/N393-D/N394 motif may contribute to function, though alanine scanning did not identify this motif as critical (C125).

results.result: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against West Nile virus and localizes to WNV replication sites at ER-derived membranes marked by PDIA3 and dsRNA. p46 may be recruited from the Golgi to WNV replication sites during infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56, C141-C145 are supported by viral titer data (Figure 6A) and confocal microscopy showing p46 colocalization with PDIA3 and dsRNA during WNV infection (Figure 6B-D). The decreased association with Golgin-97 during infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and localization to ZIKV replication sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) support the model of p46 recruitment to flavivirus replication organelles.

results.result: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against CVB3 compared to p42, suggesting broad activity against picornaviruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C147 are supported by viral RNA and titer quantification data (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) showing significant reduction in CVB3 replication by p46 but not p42. This extends the findings from EMCV to another picornavirus.

results.result: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2 compared to p42, with 25-fold reduction in viral titer. This enhanced activity depends on the CaaX motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by viral titer data in ACE2-expressing 293T cells (Figure 6F) showing that p46 has 5-fold greater activity than p42, and that p46ATIL (CaaX mutant) has reduced activity similar to p42. This demonstrates that endomembrane targeting is critical for p46 activity against SARS-CoV-2.

results.result: OAS1 p42 and p46 do not significantly impact replication of IAV or VSV, viruses that do not replicate on endomembrane organelles. This suggests p46 is specifically antiviral against viruses using the endomembrane system for replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by viral RNA and titer data for IAV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-F) and flow cytometry data for VSV-GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) showing no significant antiviral effect of either isoform. This specificity supports the model that p46's enhanced activity is due to its endomembrane localization providing access to viruses replicating at these sites.

results.result: The G allele at rs10774671 encoding OAS1 p46 is associated with protection from severe COVID-19. Association was detected in two independent cohorts with p=0.017 (OR 0.35) and p=7.38x10⁻⁷ (OR 0.80).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C65-C67, C78 are supported by genetic association data from a local cohort of 34 severe cases and 99 controls (Figure 6G, Supplementary file 5) and replication in a UK cohort of 1676 cases and 8380 controls. The consistent protective effect of the G allele across cohorts, combined with in vitro data showing enhanced p46 activity against SARS-CoV-2, provides strong support for this association.

results.result: The SNP rs10774671 (A>G) controls production of OAS1 isoforms. The A allele produces primarily p42, the G allele produces p46, and heterozygotes produce both isoforms.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C101-C106, C108-C109 are supported by genotyping data and immunoblot analysis across multiple cell lines (Figure 1B) and PBMCs from donors with different genotypes (Figure 1C). The data clearly demonstrate the genotype-phenotype relationship for OAS1 isoform expression.

results.result: Human OAS1 is alternatively spliced to produce isoforms p42, p44, p46, p48, and p52. All isoforms share the first five exons containing RNA binding and catalytic domains. Under the experimental conditions used, primarily p42 and p46 were observed, with p44, p48, and p52 being weakly expressed or unstable.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C107, C110-C111 are supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), immunoblot data showing primarily p42 and p46 expression (Figure 1B-C), and citations to previous literature documenting instability of other isoforms. The observation that p46 is expressed more strongly than p42 in heterozygotes is noted but not mechanistically explained.

results.result: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini, suggesting the CaaX motif has a conserved role in OAS1 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) showing conservation of the CaaX motif across vertebrate species. However, the functional significance of this conservation is inferred rather than directly tested across species.

results.result: The G allele at rs10774671 is ancestral and prevalent in African populations, while the A allele is prevalent outside Africa. The G allele was reintroduced into Homo sapiens by Neanderthal introgression.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by population genetics data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and citation to previous genetic studies on Neanderthal introgression. The population distribution data is descriptive and well-documented.

results.result: The SNP rs10774671 is in high linkage disequilibrium with the lead GWAS SNP rs10735079 (D'=0.91, r²=0.79). Both SNPs are expression and splicing QTL for OAS1 and OAS3, suggesting the association with COVID-19 may affect both splicing and expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81, C153 are supported by linkage disequilibrium analysis and citation to QTL data. However, the relative contributions of splicing versus expression changes to COVID-19 protection are not experimentally determined in this study.

results.result: Background on the OAS/RNase L pathway: OAS proteins are IFN-induced sensors of viral dsRNA that synthesize 2′-5′A, which activates RNase L to cleave viral and cellular RNA. The human OAS family comprises OAS1, OAS2, and OAS3 with different domain structures and RNA binding capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C89-C93 are supported by citations to established literature on the OAS/RNase L pathway. These are well-established background facts that provide context for the study.

results.result: Background on virus replication strategies: Positive-strand RNA viruses (flaviviruses, picornaviruses, coronaviruses) replicate within modified organelles of the endomembrane system, which shields viral RNA from cytosolic sensors. Different viruses use different organelle membranes (ER, Golgi). Negative-strand RNA viruses like IAV and VSV replicate in the nucleus or cytosol respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17, C113-C114, C119, C140, C146, C148-C150, C152 are supported by citations to established literature on viral replication strategies. These are well-documented facts that provide rationale for the study's hypothesis.

results.result: Background on genetic associations: The rs10774671 SNP is associated with susceptibility to flaviviruses and autoimmune disorders. Other innate immune genes (IFNAR2, TYK2) are associated with severe COVID-19. The type I IFN pathway may be compromised in severe COVID-19 patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C77, C85, C87, C96 are supported by citations to previous genetic association studies and COVID-19 research. These provide context for the genetic findings but are not novel results of this study.

results.result: Summary conclusion: Endomembrane targeting of OAS1 p46 confers enhanced antiviral activity against viruses using the endomembrane system for replication, while p42 has comparatively weak activity against these viruses. Subcellular localization determines antiviral specificity of OAS proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C94 are summary statements supported by the collective experimental data showing enhanced p46 activity against EMCV, WNV, CVB3, and SARS-CoV-2 but not IAV or VSV, along with mechanistic data on localization and RNA binding. These represent the main conclusions of the study.

results.result: Mechanistic model and speculation: The authors propose that prenylated p46 localizes to organelle membranes and is incorporated into viral replication organelles during infection, enhancing access to viral RNA. They speculate about viral evasion strategies and the difficulty of viruses evolving away from endomembrane replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75, C154-C156, C160 are largely speculative proposals about mechanisms and viral evolution. While the model is consistent with the data, direct evidence for p46 incorporation into VROs, continuous recruitment during infection, and constraints on viral evolution are not provided. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future testing rather than established findings.

results.result: Interpretations and implications: The authors propose that p46's enhanced activity explains the genetic association with COVID-19 protection, that 2′-5′A locally activates RNase L at replication sites, that positioning sensors at different subcellular sites allows response to diverse viral strategies, and that strong selective pressures impact OAS1 SNP prevalence.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C86, C88, C95, C97-C98 are interpretations and implications of the data rather than direct findings. While plausible and supported by the overall results, these represent inferences about mechanism, evolution, and broader immune strategy that would require additional experiments to definitively establish.

results.result: Speculation on viral antagonism: MHV and MERS-CoV encode phosphodiesterases that degrade 2′-5′A, but SARS-CoV-2 lacks this enzyme, potentially making it susceptible to OAS1 p46.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C159 are based on knowledge of viral genomes and inference about susceptibility. While C157 is established knowledge and C158 is factually correct about SARS-CoV-2 genome content, C159 is speculative. The enhanced activity of p46 against SARS-CoV-2 is demonstrated, but whether this is specifically due to lack of phosphodiesterase is not tested.

results.result: Background on RNase L and OAS1 oligomerization: RNase L cleavage products can activate RIG-I/MDA5. OAS1 tetramerization is required for 2′-5′A synthesis. The CFK motif is critical for oligomerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C118, C128, C45 are supported by citations to established literature. These provide mechanistic context for understanding OAS1 function but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Alanine scanning of the p46 C-terminus: None of the hexameric alanine substitution mutants affected viral RNA levels as strongly as CaaX disruption. The E392-E/N393-D/N394 motif is conserved in mammalian OAS1 p46 orthologs, and mutant 8 affecting this region showed slight decrease in Golgi colocalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 are supported by viral RNA quantification data (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and microscopy data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C). However, the functional significance of the E-E/N-D/N motif remains unclear since the alanine substitution did not significantly affect antiviral activity, creating some uncertainty about its importance.

results.result: Characterization of p46 mutants: Mutation of the CFK motif does not alter localization of p42 or p46. All p46 truncation mutants localize to the Golgi, though the Δ32aa mutant shows slightly decreased correlation with Golgi markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-I). These findings help separate the effects of oligomerization from localization and demonstrate that even short C-termini can support Golgi targeting when a CaaX motif is present.

results.result: Conclusions about p46 structure-function: OAS1 p46 proteins might oligomerize aided by CaaX-mediated membrane localization. The unique C-terminal region including oligomerization and prenylation motifs is maintained across vertebrates, presumably because it displays the strongest antiviral activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 are supported by experimental data on CFK mutants and membrane localization, and sequence conservation data. However, C163 includes speculation about evolutionary selection ('presumably because') that, while reasonable, is not directly tested. The inference about oligomerization at membranes (C161) is supported by the data but represents a model rather than direct observation.

results.result: Many positive-strand RNA viruses depend on lipid products of the mevalonate pathway or prenylation for replication and cannot broadly antagonize this pathway.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is supported by citations to established literature on viral dependence on lipid metabolism. This provides rationale for why membrane-targeted immune sensors might be difficult for viruses to evade.
